{{short description|Geometric theorem}}
[[File:Crossbar theorem diagram.svg|thumbnail|The Crossbar Theorem says ray AD intersects segment BC]]
<span lang="fa" dir="ltr">In</span> [[geometry]], the '''crossbar theorem''' states that if ray AD is between [[Line_(mathematics)#Ray|ray]] AC and ray AB, then ray AD intersects [[line segment]] BC.<ref>{{harvnb|Greenberg|1974|loc=p. 69}}</ref> 

This result is one of the deeper results in axiomatic plane geometry.<ref>{{harvnb|Kay|1993|loc=p. 122}}</ref> It is often used in proofs to justify the statement that a line through a vertex of a triangle lying ''inside'' the triangle meets the side of the triangle opposite that vertex. This property was often used by Euclid in his proofs without explicit justification.<ref>{{harvnb|Blau|2003|loc=p. 135}}</ref>

Some modern treatments (not Euclid's) of the proof of the theorem that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent start like this: Let ABC be a triangle with side AB congruent to side AC. ''Draw the angle bisector of angle A and let D be the point at which it meets side BC''. And so on. The justification for the existence of point D is the often unstated crossbar theorem. For this particular result, other proofs exist which do not require the use of the crossbar theorem.<ref>{{harvnb|Moise|1974|loc=p. 70}}</ref>
